content: Castor oil is a powerful cathartic substance derived from the bean of the castor plant. Historical accounts, dating back to ancient Egypt, have suggested its use as a means to stimulate labor. In midwifery practice, castor oil has been traditionally employed to initiate labor, although its exact mechanism of action in this context remains poorly understood. Clinical trial data evaluating its efficacy for this purpose are limited. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of castor oil or enemas on cervical ripening or labor induction during the third trimester, comparing these methods to other established techniques for labor induction. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of April 30, 2013) and relevant bibliographies. The review included clinical trials that compared castor oil, baths, or enemas with placebo, no treatment, or other predefined labor induction methods. Three clinical trials, involving a total of 233 women, were included in the analysis. The results showed no significant differences in cesarean section rates between castor oil and other interventions in the two trials that reported this outcome (risk ratio [RR] 2.04, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.92 to 4.55). Additionally, no data were available regarding neonatal or maternal mortality or morbidity. There was no evidence of a difference between castor oil and placebo/no treatment in terms of instrumental delivery rates, the presence of meconium-stained amniotic fluid, or Apgar scores below seven at five minutes. However, the small sample size of the included studies limited the ability to detect anything other than large differences in outcomes. One notable finding was that all women who ingested castor oil experienced nausea (RR 59.92, 95% CI 8.46 to 424.52). This side effect was consistently reported across the studies. The authors concluded that the three trials included in this review involved small sample sizes and used single doses of castor oil. The methodological quality of these studies was suboptimal, introducing a risk of bias. As a result, the findings should be interpreted with caution. Further research is necessary to better quantify the efficacy and safety of castor oil as an agent for cervical ripening and labor induction.
